nodes.body: The platform clock had stopped at eleven minutes past midnight, though the hour hand seemed to be inching backward. {~HERO:Vera~} stepped around a frozen puddle and pulled the collar of her coat tighter. The last northbound overnight train of the season was already breathing steam into the switching yard, its windows a row of dim amber rectangles against the sleet. No whistle had blown. No voice had called her name. The sleet softened to full snow as she lifted her case and climbed the iron step, and the carriage received her with a long, slow exhalation of heated air that smelled of wool and old coffee. The door swung shut behind her on its own, and the train began to move before she had chosen a direction.

choices.label: Find a seat and take it in.

nodes.body: The carriage was half-empty and entirely strange. Four ways forward presented themselves at once, each one a different quality of silence: the night conductor standing very still at the far end with something gleaming at his hip; the long corridor of curtained sleepers swaying to the left; a folded paper resting on the seat opposite, its crease sharp as a fresh wound; and the wide country beyond the glass, a black scroll unscrolling behind the snow. The carriage sways and the cold glass holds her reflection over the dark. Vera could feel the night waiting for her to commit to one direction.

choices.label: Watch the night land go by.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the night conductor and his silver punch-clock. He stood at the threshold of the next carriage, neither welcoming nor blocking the way, his uniform pressed with an exactness that belonged to an earlier century. His fingers rested on the punch-clock without moving; the device's face was a small moon of polished nickel, its dial unreadable from where she stood. The carriage sways and the cold glass holds her reflection over the dark, a ghost laid over the snow-lit fields beyond. Something about the conductor's stillness was not patience. It was the stillness of a thing that had been waiting longer than a single journey could account for. The silver clock caught the overhead lamp and held it.

{~HERO:Vera~} could see, now, that the night conductor's silver punch-clock had no hands. Where the hands should have been, the metal surface was perfectly smooth, as though they had never been fitted. The conductor's face above it was lined in a way that shifted with the swaying of the carriage: young from one angle, ancient from another. His uniform jacket bore a name stitched in thread too fine to read. The last northbound overnight train of the season seemed to hold its breath around her. She could step forward now and ask a question, risk whatever attention that would draw. Or she could withdraw to a seat nearby and let the night teach her this man's purpose in its own time. The choice was hers, but the carriage would not wait forever.

choices.label: Sit nearby and watch him work.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} walked straight up to the night conductor and asked what time the train was due at the north terminus. He raised his silver punch-clock and held it toward her like an offering. It was warm, almost hot, and when she looked into the blank face she saw her own reflection laid over a depth that had no bottom. His voice, when it came, was dry as old paper: 'This train keeps no hour you would recognise.' She felt the fact burrow down behind her ribs and lodge there, a splinter of certainty in a night made of fog. It was not an answer she could unwrap now; it was a key to a door further along the train. The last northbound overnight train of the season had just become a question with a name.

choices.label: Carry his answer forward with you.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} took a seat three rows back from the night conductor, close enough to study him, far enough that his attention did not land on her. She watched the way his thumb rested on the silver punch-clock, a habitual pressure that looked like a comfort, or a restraint. The carriage filled with the low hum of wheels on welded rail. The snow had thickened against the glass. She could keep this observation, turn this one detail over through the rest of the night until it found its place among the other wrong things the train was offering her. Or she could let the deep rhythm of the track and the warmth of the carriage pull her down into a half-sleep, the conductor's secret dissolving into dream before she had truly held it. The night was long, but her attention was not infinite.

choices.label: Hold the thread and stay alert.
Let the hour take you under.

nodes.body: The small wrongness was this: the night conductor's silver punch-clock was not a timepiece at all. It was a housing. Inside, glimpsed for half a second when the carriage lurched through a switch, {~HERO:Vera~} saw not gears but a coil of something organic, dark and slowly turning, like a root growing in accelerated quiet. Her mind snagged on the image and would not let it go. The journey closed around the discovery like the walls of a room shifting inward by an inch she could feel but not measure. The conductor did not look at her, but she understood he knew she had seen. The whole length of the carriage was holding its breath.

{~HERO:Vera~} moved away from the conductor, carrying the image of the turning thing in the clock like a stone in her palm. Each sliding door she pushed through into the next car seemed heavier than the last. The windows gave back nothing but the snowfall and her own face, older in the glass than she remembered being. She was coming to understand that the last northbound overnight train of the season was not built around a destination. It was built around a question, and the question sat ahead of her in the dark, waiting for her to arrive at it. She walked on.

choices.label: Follow the question to the pivot.

nodes.body: The sound of the wheels rose and engulfed her, a soft roar that smoothed the edges of her attention until the conductor and his silver clock dissolved into the grain of the dark. {~HERO:Vera~} surfaced later with a start, her cheek pressed to cold glass, the carriage empty of him. She was safe. The train was still moving north. But the splinter of certainty she had briefly held was gone, and the place behind her ribs where it had lodged felt hollowed out. She had missed the moment, and the night would not offer it twice. Outside, the snow fell on land that looked no different than it had an hour ago.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the long row of curtained sleeper berths. Heavy green drapes hung from brass rods, each curtain drawn tight, each berth a pocket of private darkness. No sound came from behind them—not a cough, not the rustle of a blanket, not the soft rhythm of sleeping breath. The carriage sways and the cold glass holds her reflection over the dark. She noticed, with a small tightening in her chest, that the berth curtains were not still. They moved slightly, as though something inside each compartment was pressing gently outward, then releasing, in a rhythm that did not match the train's motion.

{~HERO:Vera~} stood in the aisle between the long row of curtained sleeper berths. She could see now that the brass numbers above each compartment were not sequential. They jumped: 3, 7, 22, 9, 1. And some of the numbers were worn almost smooth while others looked newly struck, bright against the dark wood. The breathing behind the curtains had not stopped. She could part a curtain now and see what lay on the other side—risk whatever wakefulness was waiting behind the green cloth. Or she could sit here, let the rhythm of the berths become part of the night's texture, and let the last northbound overnight train of the season decide when—and if—it would reveal what it was carrying.

choices.label: Sit and wait among the berths.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} reached up and drew the curtain of berth number 9 aside. The bunk was empty, the sheets stretched tight as a hospital cot. But the pillow held the deep indentation of a head, and on the blanket lay a single pressed flower, still faintly blue, its petals cool and slightly damp. She did not touch it. The berth had been slept in recently—moments ago—and the sleeper had left no other trace. No bag, no coat, no shoes. The flower was not a thing a passenger would forget. It was a thing a passenger would leave. The fact settled into her mind and would not sit still; this train was carrying absences, not people, and it wanted her to notice.

{~HERO:Vera~} did not touch the curtains. She took a seat at the end of the sleeper carriage, where a small fold-down stool faced the aisle, and watched. The breathing behind the berths slowly became one sound, a single respiration that swelled and ebbed through the whole length of the car. She could let this observation settle, add it to the accumulating catalogue of wrongnesses the train was showing her, and step back into the corridor with a sharper eye. Or she could close her own eyes, here on the stool, and let the carriage's strange collective respiration carry her off. The warmth was deep and the hour was late, and the border between watching and dreaming was already thinning.

choices.label: Keep the thread and walk on.
Let the hour close your eyes.

nodes.body: The small wrongness converged on a single fact: there were no shoes. Under every curtain, at the foot of each berth where a pair of shoes should have rested on the carpet, there was only empty floor. No boots, no slippers, no scuffed leather. The train was carrying sleepers who had left their feet bare. {~HERO:Vera~} felt the discovery settle over the carriage like a bell jar lowered from the ceiling. The breathing behind the curtains did not alter, but the quality of the silence changed. She was being allowed to see. The journey had closed around this new knowledge and was holding it still for her to examine.

{~HERO:Vera~} left the sleeper car carrying the image of all those bare soles, rows of them, unseen but certain. She understood now that the last northbound overnight train of the season was collecting something from its passengers, something they had agreed to give up without knowing what it was. The question the whole train seemed built around was not waiting at the end of the line; it was threaded through every carriage, a single long nerve she was tracing hand over hand. She moved forward into the next car, toward the nerve's centre.

The breathing of the berths rose around her like water, warm and insistent, and {~HERO:Vera~} felt her own breath slow to match the rhythm of the curtains. She did not remember closing her eyes. When she opened them again her neck was stiff and the carriage was quiet in a different way—a held, settled quiet, the kind that follows a departure. The berth curtains hung flat. Whatever had been breathing behind them was finished. She was safe. The train was still moving. But the moment when the truth had been reachable had passed, and she would ride on knowing only that she had been close enough to touch it and had instead let it slip beneath the surface.

ending.title: A Door You Did Not Open

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the letter a stranger left folded on the seat. The paper was heavy, cream-coloured, the fold sharp as a blade. No envelope, no address—just her name written on the outside in a hand she did not know. The ink was dark and slightly raised, still damp in the cold air. The carriage sways and the cold glass holds her reflection over the dark. She lifted the letter and felt its weight: heavier than paper should be. Something inside the fold shifted, not loose exactly, but alive in the way a held breath is alive.

{~HERO:Vera~} held the letter a stranger left folded on her seat, and the paper was warmer than the carriage air. She could feel the grain of the fibres against her fingertips, something handwritten on the inside pressing faintly outward. The light in the carriage had dimmed, or her attention had narrowed so fully that the world beyond the paper ceased to register. She could open it now, read whatever the stranger had set down for her, and accept the risk of being seen reading it by whoever else was riding this train. Or she could tuck it into her coat and wait. Let the letter become a companion to the night, its contents still held in possibility, the last northbound overnight train of the season keeping one more secret for a while longer.

{~HERO:Vera~} opened the letter. The handwriting was small, precise, and written in a brown ink that smelled faintly of earth. It was not a message to her. It was a message about her—a description of a young woman boarding the last northbound train, carrying a case in her left hand, hesitating on the platform step. The description ended mid-sentence, at the moment the door closed behind her. There was no signature. The page was dated the day before. Whoever had written it had known she would be here, and had written her into the train before she had decided to board. The fact lodged in her mind like a needle; she was not a passenger so much as a part of the journey that had been anticipated.

{~HERO:Vera~} folded the letter into her coat pocket and let it rest there, a small warm weight against her ribs. She could keep the letter unread, let its mystery accompany her through the night, and see whether the train itself would supply the context the paper withheld. Or she could surrender to the deep hour, the endless sway of the carriage, the way the lamps had dimmed to a honeyed glow that made her eyelids heavy. The letter would still be there when she woke. Wouldn't it? The train rocked gently over a joint in the rail, and the question hung unanswered.

choices.label: Keep the letter and stay awake.

nodes.body: The small wrongness crystallised: the letter a stranger left folded on the seat had been written on paper taken from a timetable. On the reverse of the page, visible when she held it to the window light, were columns of station names printed in the railway's official type, but every station had been struck through with a single line—except one. The last entry. Not a name she recognised, but a word in a language she almost understood. The journey closed around the page like a fist gently tightening. The letter was not a message. It was a ticket stub, proof that someone had ridden this train to its real terminus and had come back.

{~HERO:Vera~} carried the letter with the struck-through stations against her heart and walked on through the swaying cars. The train was no longer a vehicle. It was a system of clues laid out in sleeping passengers and folded paper and a conductor who would not meet her eyes. The question the whole train seemed built around had a shape now, and the shape was a route that ended somewhere north of every map she had ever seen. She stepped through the next sliding door, and the air grew colder.

The letter grew heavy in her hand, heavier than its paper could explain. {~HERO:Vera~} tried to read it again—the words were still there, she could see the shapes of them—but they would not resolve into meaning. The ink seemed to deepen, to pull the lamplight into itself, until the page was a dark rectangle swimming before her eyes. She surfaced later with the letter fallen to the floor, the writing vanished entirely. She was safe. The train was still moving. But the stranger's message, the foreknowledge of her own journey, was gone, and she held only blank paper. The thing she had almost understood had sealed itself back into the night.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the black country sliding past the window. The land beyond the glass was not empty; it was full of forms that refused to resolve. Ridges that might be mountains, or might be the shoulders of something larger, sleeping. Trees that leaned into the wind and then, when she looked again, were not trees at all but telegraph poles, their wires sagging with the weight of snow. The carriage sways and the cold glass holds her reflection over the dark, a pale mask laid across the moving world. She noticed, between one pole and the next, that the moon had changed position. It was behind a cloud a moment ago. Now it was low and red and looking back.

choices.label: Press your face to the cold glass.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} could see now that the dark country outside was not country at all. It was a landscape drawn from memory and slightly wrong: a barn with a roof sloping the wrong way, a river running uphill for half a mile before fixing itself. The tracks ran through a place that had not quite finished taking shape. She could stare into this scene and force it to make sense—trace the river to its start, count the barn's windows—and risk being seen by whatever mind was dreaming this place into being. Or she could let the strange land unspool at its own pace, accept its oddness as just a part of the night, and let the last northbound overnight train of the season carry her on without demanding answers.

choices.label: Let the land be strange and move on.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} fixed her eyes on the river that ran uphill and forced herself to follow it. Her eyes burned with the effort. The river did not change direction—but at the crest of the impossible slope, where the water should have peaked and fallen, it simply stopped. Became a line. Became the edge of a map that had not been drawn any further. Beyond that line, the land was white, featureless, an absence with texture. She understood: the last northbound overnight train of the season was running on tracks that had been laid only as far as someone's attention had reached. Whatever territory lay beyond, no one had yet imagined it. The knowledge settled into her like cold iron.

{~HERO:Vera~} let the black country slide without chasing its logic. A barn with the wrong roof; a river running uphill; the low red moon watching her back. She could let these oddities accumulate like a thin frost on the glass, not yet a pattern but the promise of one, and carry this heightened alertness forward into the train's interior. Or she could let the motion of the carriage, the warmth leaching through the window, the hour pressing on her temples, pull her down. The land would keep sliding past, strange or not strange, whether she watched or slept. The question was only whether she would still be paying attention when it finally turned into something she needed to see.

choices.label: Hold the thread and stay awake.
Let the hour pull you under.

nodes.body: The small wrongness from the window and the small wrongness from the letter—the unimagined edge of the map, the struck-through stations, the river that stopped at the line of attention—all dovetailed into a single quiet certainty. The landscape outside was not real. Or not entirely real. It was a sketch, a placeholder, a set of details laid down to give the train a context while the real purpose of the journey took place elsewhere. {~HERO:Vera~} felt the night close around this understanding like a held breath, and the glass under her fingers seemed suddenly very thin, as though she could push through it and fall into the white unimagined space beyond the river's end.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned from the window carrying the image of an unfinished world. The key question the whole train seemed built around was larger than she had guessed. It was not just about why the train kept running. It was about what the train was running through. And somewhere ahead, in a carriage she had not yet entered, that question had a voice. She walked on, moving past sleeping passengers whose faces she could not quite remember, toward the centre of the night.

The glass was cold and the seat was deep, and {~HERO:Vera~}'s head grew heavy against the window's metal frame. The black country blurred and softened, becoming a wash of shadow without edges or detail. She did not feel herself fall asleep. She surfaced later with a dry mouth and a stiff neck, the carriage brightening with the first grey light of early dawn. The window now showed only ordinary fields, ordinary trees, ordinary snow. The river that had run uphill was not there. She had missed the moment when the world was still permeable, still almost dreaming. The last northbound overnight train of the season hummed on toward a station she already knew would feel too small.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the dining-car regulars who never seem to order. Four of them sat at a table bolted to the floor: an old man with a newspaper that never turned, a woman in a green shawl whose tea had long since stopped steaming, a boy in a school blazer staring into the tabletop's grain, and a thin-shouldered man with his back to the door. There were no plates, no cups, no sign that food had ever been served in this car. The carriage swayed and the cold glass held her reflection over the dark. The old man's newspaper was dated three years ago. The woman's tea was not just cold. It was frozen solid.

The four diners did not acknowledge {~HERO:Vera~}, but she felt the weight of their attention settle on her anyway—not hostile, exactly, but curious in the way old stone might be curious about a new footprint. The table between them was set with a lace cloth gone grey with age. She could step up to them directly, ask a question, disrupt the frozen tableau and see what thawed out. Or she could take a seat at the counter across the aisle, order nothing herself, and let the regulars become accustomed to her presence. The last northbound overnight train of the season had been carrying these four for a long while. They might speak when they were ready.

choices.label: Step up and speak to them.
Sit at the counter and wait.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} walked to the table and asked the dining-car regulars where they were going. The woman in the green shawl lifted her head and {~HERO:Vera~} saw that her eyes were the same grey as the cloth, the same grey as the morning outside that had not yet arrived. 'We aren't going,' she said. 'We stay.' The boy in the blazer spoke without looking up from the tabletop. 'We got on at a station that isn't there anymore.' The thin-shouldered man at the back said nothing, but {~HERO:Vera~} saw his hands under the table: they were counting, finger to thumb, a silent tally with no end. The old man turned a page of his newspaper and the date at the top read the day {~HERO:Vera~} was born.

{~HERO:Vera~} sat at the counter and watched the dining-car regulars in the mirror behind the bar. The mirror showed the same four figures, but the woman in green was holding a cup that did not exist in the real room, and the boy in the blazer was drawing something on the tablecloth with a finger that left no mark. The regulars were not frozen, she realised. They were looped. The same small gestures, the same patterns of breath, repeating on a cycle too slow for the eye to catch easily. She could keep this observation, add it to the growing catalogue of the train's strange physics, and walk on. Or she could let the loop pull her in, let her own breathing slow to match its rhythm, and risk becoming a fifth regular at an empty table.

choices.label: Break the pull and walk on.

nodes.body: The small wrongness came together: the dining-car regulars who never seem to order were not passengers. They were remnants. People who had been riding this train so long that their original journey had worn away entirely, like the name stitched on the conductor's uniform, and all that remained was the act of riding. They were not going anywhere because they had already gone. {~HERO:Vera~} felt the journey close around this fact like a held breath, and for a moment the dining car was not a car but a waiting room in a station that had been demolished a century ago.

choices.label: Press on toward the next carriage.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} left the dining car with the image of the boy's silent counting hands and the woman's grey eyes. The question the whole train seemed built around was beginning to branch: it was not one question but a knot of them, and the regulars were a thread she would need to follow. She carried what they had taught her—the loop, the stilled tea, the date on the newspaper—and moved on through the swaying cars, toward the place where the passengers became more than passengers.

The boy in the school blazer raised his head at last and looked at {~HERO:Vera~} with eyes that were not a child's eyes. 'You're riding a long time,' he said, and his voice was old, older than the dining car, older than the rails. {~HERO:Vera~} tried to answer but the words would not come. She felt the loop settle around her, not trapping but holding—a gentle, almost tender custody. This was one true, unsettling detail: the regulars were not lost. They were keeping the train company. And she had been offered a seat at their table, whether she wanted it or not. She held the knowledge but did not join them. The night carried her forward, and she carried the boy's ancient eyes into the dawn.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the small child awake at the end of the carriage. She was perhaps six, barefoot, sitting cross-legged on a seat meant for an adult, her heels kicking softly against the upholstery. She was not playing with a toy or looking out the window. She was watching {~HERO:Vera~}. The carriage sways and the cold glass holds her reflection over the dark. The child's expression was not one of curiosity. It was recognition. She had been waiting for {~HERO:Vera~} specifically, and the waiting had not been short.

choices.label: Walk down the aisle toward her.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} stood in the aisle facing the small child awake at the end of the carriage. The girl had a blanket pulled up to her chin, though the carriage was warm, and her fingers kept pleating and unpleating the edge of it in a rhythm that was almost musical. She did not speak, but her eyes were full of something {~HERO:Vera~} could not name—not quite a warning, not quite an invitation. {~HERO:Vera~} could kneel beside the seat and ask the child directly what she was doing awake, risk the answer being larger than a question a child should be able to answer. Or she could sit in the seat opposite and simply keep her company, trusting that the night would bring the child's purpose forward when it was ready.

{~HERO:Vera~} knelt beside the small child awake at the end of the carriage and asked her name. The girl looked at her for a long moment, pleating the blanket, pleating it, and then said, 'I knew you on the platform. You were holding your case in your left hand. I was the one who held the door.' {~HERO:Vera~} had not seen her. She had not seen anyone. The platform had been empty—she was certain of that. But the girl's voice held no doubt. The fact lodged in {~HERO:Vera~}'s mind like a stone dropped into still water: she had been watched before she boarded, and the watcher had been this child, and the child had been here all along, riding ahead of her through the night, waiting for her to catch up.

{~HERO:Vera~} took the seat opposite the small child awake at the end of the carriage. She did not ask a question, and the child did not offer an answer. They sat in a shared stillness while the train rocked over a long curve and the lamps dimmed to a soft amber. {~HERO:Vera~} could feel the child's attention like a small, patient hand laid against her own mind. She could hold this peace, this wordless understanding that something important was being communicated below the level of speech, and carry it forward into the night. Or she could let the hour and the warmth and the child's steady gaze lull her into a state where the message arrived but could not be kept.

choices.label: Stay with the child and stay awake.
Let the hour take you under.

nodes.body: The small wrongness converged: the child was not a child. Or not only a child. She was the train's memory. She remembered every passenger who had ever boarded, every station the train had ever served, every night it had run. And {~HERO:Vera~} was not the first young woman travelling north alone she had waited for. 'There was another one,' the girl said, 'three winters ago. She had the same case. She didn't listen.' {~HERO:Vera~} felt the journey close around this new knowledge like a held breath. She was part of a pattern, and the pattern had a shape, and the shape led forward into the dark.

choices.label: Press on with the child's warning.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} rose from the seat across from the child and walked on. The girl did not wave or call after her; she simply returned to pleating her blanket, a small figure receding into the dimness of the carriage. What the child had told {~HERO:Vera~} was this: the question the whole train seemed built around had been asked before. And it would be asked again. But the asking—and the listening—was hers alone, tonight. She moved through the swaying cars with her shoulders set, toward the next knot of passengers and their secrets.

The child's steady gaze was the last thing {~HERO:Vera~} saw before the warmth of the carriage rose and covered her like a blanket. She did not dream, exactly. She was aware of the child's presence beside her, a small firm hand holding her sleeve, and a voice saying something she could not later recall—a string of syllables that felt like a name but was not her name. She surfaced in an empty carriage, the child gone, the blanket folded neatly on the opposite seat. One true, unsettling detail remained: the blanket was warm. The girl had been there moments ago. And {~HERO:Vera~} had missed the message. But she folded the blanket and kept it with her, and the warmth of it was real and hers to carry off the last northbound overnight train of the season.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the man softly counting stations that never come. He sat with his back very straight, hands resting on his knees, his lips moving in a whisper too low to catch. His eyes were fixed on the window, but {~HERO:Vera~} could see that the window held only the reflection of the carriage interior. No land. No snow. A mirror of the man himself, endlessly counting. The carriage sways and the cold glass holds her reflection over the dark. His lips shaped a number, then paused, then shaped it again. The same number. He was not counting forward. He was caught.

{~HERO:Vera~} could hear the man softly counting stations that never come more clearly now: a litany of names she did not recognise, spoken in an accent that belonged to a region she could not place. His voice was calm, unhurried, as though he had all night, as though the night would not end. She could interrupt him, ask what stations he was naming, and risk breaking whatever fragile machinery kept him upright in his seat. Or she could sit beside him without speaking, matching her silence to his murmur, and let the last northbound overnight train of the season reveal the man's purpose in its own way. Some truths, she was learning, dissolved under direct attention.

choices.label: Ask him what he is naming.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} put a hand on the arm of the man softly counting stations that never come and asked him plainly, 'What are you counting?' He stopped. His head turned toward her with a slowness that was almost geological. His eyes were kind and deeply tired. 'The stops,' he said. 'Every stop this train was meant to make, before the line was cut. I am the one who remembers them.' He named a station—a small town, a wooden platform, a signal lamp that burned green—and {~HERO:Vera~} felt the name settle into her like a stone. The station did not exist anymore. But the man's memory of it kept it in the timetable, and the timetable kept the train on its rails. He was not a passenger. He was a bearing wall.

choices.label: Carry what he has told you.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} did not speak. She sat beside the man softly counting stations that never come and let his murmur wash over her like a second track, a rhythm beneath the rhythm of the wheels. She did not know the names he was saying, but she began to feel them—a shape to each syllable, a weight of longing or relief. She could let this become part of the night's texture, a thread in the larger weave, and stand up when the time came to move on. Or she could let the counting pull her down into its cadence, a sleep not of exhaustion but of surrender, the names becoming a lullaby she would not remember in the morning.

choices.label: Keep the thread and rise to go.
Let the counting take you under.

nodes.body: The small wrongness came clear: the man softly counting stations that never come was not reciting from memory. He was generating. Each station name he spoke was a place that might have existed, a branch line that might have been built, a town that might have grown around a platform if someone had chosen to lay track there instead of here. He was the railway's grief. The journey closed around this understanding like a held breath, and {~HERO:Vera~} understood that every passenger on the last northbound overnight train of the season was carrying something that had been lost, and the train was the only place that loss could still travel.

choices.label: Press on with his litany in your ears.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} rose and left the counting man, but the sound of his voice followed her through the sliding doors—a thread of names, half-heard, an alternative railway stretching out behind the train in ghostly parallel. The question the whole train seemed built around was not only about where it was going. It was about where it had never been allowed to go. She walked on toward the next knot of passengers, and her own breath began to shape a name she did not yet know.

The man softly counting stations that never come paused in his recitation and looked at {~HERO:Vera~} with his tired, kind eyes. 'You're carrying a name,' he said. 'I can hear it. When you're ready to give it over, I'll add it to the route.' {~HERO:Vera~} did not know what he meant—she had no name to give—but she felt something lift in her chest, some burden she had not been aware of carrying. The man smiled and returned to his counting. He had offered her a transaction she did not fully understand, but she kept the memory of his words. It was a true, unsettling detail, and it was hers. The numbers and the names went on, but somewhere among them was a syllable that belonged to her.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the woman in grey travelling in mourning. She sat alone at a table meant for four, her hands folded around a handkerchief that had been twisted into a tight rope. Her veil was drawn, but the carriage lamps caught the outline of her face beneath it: still, composed, a figure from an older photograph. The carriage sways and the cold glass holds her reflection over the dark. On the seat beside her rested a small wooden box, no larger than a book, its lid closed. {~HERO:Vera~} felt the weight of it before she understood why.

{~HERO:Vera~} stood before the woman in grey travelling in mourning. The woman's veil stirred with her breath, a faint inward-outward that did not disturb the fabric enough to reveal her eyes. The box on the seat beside her was carved with a pattern of leaves, almost worn smooth by handling. {~HERO:Vera~} could speak now, offer condolences or ask directly what the woman was carrying and where she was going—risk intruding on a grief that was none of her business. The living owed them patience.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} sat down opposite the woman in grey travelling in mourning and asked, 'May I sit with you?' The woman lifted her veil with a hand that was younger than {~HERO:Vera~} expected, unlined and steady, and her eyes were the colour of rain on slate. 'You may,' she said. 'The journey is long, and the company is thin.' {~HERO:Vera~} asked where she was travelling to, and the woman placed her hand on the small wooden box. 'I am taking my daughter home. She was born on this line. She died on this line. I ride it once a season, and the train remembers her with me.' The fact landed in {~HERO:Vera~}'s chest like a stone into deep water: the train did not only carry the living. It carried the dead, and it carried the ones who loved them, and the journey was a form of tending.

{~HERO:Vera~} did not speak. She sat across from the woman in grey travelling in mourning and let the silence between them fill with the sound of the wheels. The woman's hands never stilled on the handkerchief, twisting, untwisting, but {~HERO:Vera~} saw that the motion was not anxious—it was rhythmic, a private observance, like the counting man's litany. She could let this shared stillness become part of what she carried, a quiet understanding that some passengers were riding for reasons that could not be explained aloud. Or she could let the hour and the woman's steady, sorrowful dignity lull her into a state where she stopped learning and simply floated, the content of the box remaining a mystery she would never solve.

choices.label: Keep the silence and stay awake.

nodes.body: The small wrongness crystallised: the box on the seat beside the woman in grey travelling in mourning was not a box. It was a ticket. Carved with the route of the line, leaf by leaf, a map of a journey made in reverse, from terminus to origin. The woman was not accompanying the dead. She was delivering them. And the train was the courier. {~HERO:Vera~} felt the journey close around this truth like a held breath, and for a moment the whole carriage seemed to dim, as though the lamps themselves were bowing their heads.

{~HERO:Vera~} rose from the table and left the woman in grey to her observance. The question the whole train seemed built around had deepened again: it was not only a question for the living. It was a question the dead had asked first. She walked on through the swaying cars, the image of the leaf-carved box burning gently at the back of her mind, toward the place where the train would ask her, at last, to choose.

The woman in grey travelling in mourning reached across the table and took {~HERO:Vera~}'s hand. Her fingers were cold, but the cold was not unkind. 'You are also carrying something,' she said. 'I can feel it. You have been carrying it a long time, and you do not know its name yet.' {~HERO:Vera~} tried to answer, but her throat closed. The woman pressed something into her palm—a small smooth thing, a pebble or a seed, warm from the woman's own hand—and then withdrew. 'When you know its name,' she said, 'you may give it to the train.' {~HERO:Vera~} held the gift and did not open her hand. One true, unsettling detail, and it was real, and it was hers to carry off the last northbound overnight train of the season.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the conductor pressed a second time near the tunnel. He had moved. He was no longer at the head of the carriage but here, beside the door that led into the baggage car, as though he had been waiting for her to pass. His silver punch-clock was cradled in both hands, and the surface of it was no longer blank. A single mark had appeared—a hairline scratch, or a seam. The carriage sways and the cold glass holds her reflection over the dark. The conductor's face was older now, the lines deeper, the collar of his uniform slightly frayed. He looked like a man who had been riding this train for a hundred years and had only just begun to feel the weight of it.

{~HERO:Vera~} faced the conductor pressed a second time near the tunnel. He did not speak, but his silence was different now—not withholding, but expectant. He was waiting for her to ask the right question. The scratch on the punch-clock's face glinted in the lamplight, and {~HERO:Vera~} understood that the clock was opening, slowly, in response to something she had done—or something she had learned.
