Or she could let him keep his silence a while longer, trusting that the mountain ahead would force the truth out generation by generation.

choices.label: Wait for the mountain to press the truth out.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} asked the conductor directly, 'What is this train really carrying?' His face did not change, but the punch-clock in his hands gave a soft click, like a lock disengaging. 'Whatever the passengers bring aboard,' he said. 'Grief, memory, unfinished journeys. The ones that have no station left to receive them. The train holds them until they are ready to be set down. I am only the keeper of the clock that measures the holding.' {~HERO:Vera~} heard the fact and felt it settle into her like frost on a window. The train was not a vehicle. It was a vessel. And the vessel was nearing its farthest point north—the tunnel where some things were laid to rest and others were asked to continue.

{~HERO:Vera~} did not press the conductor. She stood with him in the vestibule, the two of them swaying together as the train climbed toward the mountain. She could feel the weight of the rock ahead, the way the rails were bending toward a darkness that had nothing to do with the hour. She could hold this patience, let the tunnel force the conductor's hand, and emerge on the far side with whatever truth the mountain wrung from him. Or she could let the climb and the cold and the conductor's steady, ancient presence lull her into a state where she accepted the mystery without solving it, arriving at the far side of the night with nothing but a sense of having been close to something vast.

choices.label: Hold the thread and stay alert.

nodes.body: The small wrongness came clear: the conductor pressed a second time near the tunnel was not a man. He was a layer. Peel back the uniform and there was another uniform beneath it, older, from another railway, another century. Peel back the face and there was another face. He was the accumulated watchfulness of every conductor who had ever ridden a last train north, layered one over the other like sediment. And the punch-clock was opening because the sediment was shifting. {~HERO:Vera~} felt the journey close around this understanding like a held breath, and the mountain ahead seemed to lean toward the train as though listening.

{~HERO:Vera~} left the conductor in the vestibule, his many faces settling one over the other like a deck of cards being squared. The question the whole train seemed built around was no longer a riddle. It was a responsibility. The tunnel was coming, and the tunnel was the place where the vessel opened and what it carried was offered back to the mountain. She walked on through the swaying cars, the walls of the carriage seeming to contract around her as the ceiling pressed lower, toward the dark mouth ahead.

The conductor pressed a second time near the tunnel opened his mouth as though to speak, and {~HERO:Vera~} saw that inside it was the night sky. Stars. A cold, clear blackness with no train, no rails, no mountain. Just the silence between the stars and the distant, rhythmic pulse of something vast and indifferent. He closed his mouth again. He had not spoken, but she had seen. One true, unsettling detail—the conductor was a doorway, and he had shown her the other side. It did not complete the picture. It did not explain where the train was going. But it was real, and it was hers. She carried the image of that star-filled mouth off the last northbound overnight train of the season and into whatever morning waited.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the faint map inked in the margins of the letter. She had not noticed it before—not fully. The main text of the letter consumed attention, but the margins held a web of thin lines, station names in miniature, directional arrows drawn with a nib so fine they looked like spider silk. The lines formed a route that did not match any official railway map. It curved north, yes, but then it kept going—off the edge of the paper, off the edge of any geography {~HERO:Vera~} knew. The carriage sways and the cold glass holds her reflection over the dark. The map was still being drawn. As she watched, a new line inched outward from a junction labelled only with a symbol that might have been a bird, or a flame.

choices.label: Trace the map with your finger.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} held the faint map inked in the margins of the letter under the lamplight. The ink was the same brown as the letter's text—that faint earthy smell—and the paper was warm where the lines had most recently been drawn. The map was not a record of a journey taken. It was a record of a journey in progress. And the journey was hers. She could see her own route marked on it now: the platform, the sleeper car, the dining car, the child's seat. Everything she had already passed through was fixed in ink. Everything ahead was still pale, tentative, the lines branching and rebranching as though the map itself did not yet know which way she would choose. She could follow the map's suggestions, or she could fold the letter away and trust her own instincts.

choices.label: Study the map and follow its hint.
Fold the letter and trust yourself.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} studied the faint map inked in the margins of the letter and saw, at the far upper corner, a destination marked in a different hand—hers. Her own handwriting, her own name for a place she had never seen. The map was not predicting her route. It was reflecting it. Her choices were being drawn onto the page as she made them, by some agency that knew her mind before she had fully spoken it to herself. The fact settled into her like a cold current: she was not alone in her own head. The train, or the letter, or whatever intelligence had written her boarding before she boarded, was also writing her destination. And it was waiting for her to decide whether to accept the destination it offered or choose a different one.

{~HERO:Vera~} refolded the letter with the faint map still hidden in its margins and put it back in her pocket. She did not need the map. She was already on the route. The lines would draw themselves whether she watched them or not. She could let the letter remain a mystery, a companion she did not fully understand, and trust that whatever intelligence was sketching her journey would keep sketching it regardless. Or she could let the hour and the warmth and the gentle pressure of the folded paper against her ribs lull her into a state where the map's meaning washed over her without being grasped.

choices.label: Hold the map in reserve and stay awake.
Let the night dissolve the lines.

nodes.body: The small wrongness revealed itself: the faint map inked in the margins of the letter was not a map of the railway. It was a map of {~HERO:Vera~}. Every line corresponded to a memory, every station to a moment of loss or decision in her own life, translated into the language of track and switch and signal. The stranger who left the letter had not been writing about her. They had been writing her. And the map was the key to reading herself as a route. The journey closed around this revelation like a held breath, and {~HERO:Vera~} understood that the tunnel ahead was not only the mountain's darkness. It was the darkness inside her own history, and she was about to enter it.

{~HERO:Vera~} walked on, holding the map of herself close to her heart. The whole train seemed built around a single question, but that question had turned inward. It was not about what the train was. It was about what she was as she rode it. The mountain ahead was waiting to ask her something only she could answer. She moved through the swaying cars, walls narrowing and ceilings pressing lower, toward the place where the rails entered the stone.

The ink of the faint map inked in the margins of the letter began to blur. Warmth from her hand, or condensation from the window, or simply the hour—something was dissolving the lines. {~HERO:Vera~} tried to trace them back, to fix the route in memory, but the map was fading faster than she could read it. Stations she had passed through, moments she had lived, all softening into a grey wash. She surfaced later with the letter gone from her hand, the map a ghost of itself, no longer readable. She was safe. The train was still moving. But the record of her own journey had been erased, and she carried only the blank margin, the empty paper. The thing she had almost understood had been reclaimed by the night.

ending.title: The Ink Runs in the Cold

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the signal lamps burning ahead of the tunnel mouth. Two lamps, one above the other, mounted on an iron post that leaned slightly into the wind. The upper lamp was red—a deep, arterial red that seemed to pulse rather than shine. The lower lamp was not lit. Or rather, it was lit with a light {~HERO:Vera~} could not name: a colour between green and absence, a colour that made her eyes ache when she tried to hold it. The carriage sways and the cold glass holds her reflection over the dark. The tunnel mouth itself was a perfect black arch in the mountainside, and the rails ran into it like a sentence disappearing into a period.

choices.label: Go closer to the signal lamps.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} stood in the vestibule, the cold air leaking through the door seals, watching the signal lamps burning ahead of the tunnel mouth. The red lamp was a warning—she understood that instinctively. The lower lamp, the unnameable colour, was something else. It was not a warning. It was a question. She could lean out into the cold and try to read the signal as a conductor would read it, decode its meaning in the railway's old language of colour and position. Or she could let the lamps remain what they were—beautiful and inscrutable—and trust that the train itself knew which signal to obey. The last northbound overnight train of the season was approaching the mountain tunnel, and the lamps had been burning here longer than any timetable could account for.

choices.label: Try to read the signal's meaning.
Let the lamps burn without translating them.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} forced herself to look directly at the lower lamp, the unnameable colour. Her eyes burned, her vision swam, but she held it. And the colour resolved. It was not a colour. It was a distance. The lamp was showing her the far side of the tunnel—not an image, but a felt distance, a length of dark that would take exactly one night to cross. The red lamp above it was not a stop signal. It was the colour of the journey she had already made. The lower lamp was the journey ahead, still unlit, waiting for her to decide what colour it would burn. The fact lodged in her mind: she was not approaching a signal. She was the signal.

{~HERO:Vera~} let the signal lamps burning ahead of the tunnel mouth remain what they were: a mystery she did not need to solve. The red lamp and the unnameable lamp, burning side by side, were not speaking to her. They were speaking to the rails, or to the mountain, or to the train itself. She could let them be part of the night's texture, an image to carry without comprehension, and trust that the crossing would teach her what she needed to know. Or she could let the cold and the dark and the steady, hypnotic pulse of the red lamp pull her into a state where she stopped asking what the signals meant and simply let them wash over her.

choices.label: Keep the image and stay alert.
Let the lamps pull you under.

nodes.body: The small wrongness resolved: the signal lamps burning ahead of the tunnel mouth were not lit by electricity or flame. They were lit by the train's approach. They had been dark until the last northbound overnight train of the season came onto the long approach curve, and they would go dark again once it passed. The lamps were a reflection of the journey, not a direction to it. {~HERO:Vera~} felt the night close around this understanding like a held breath. She was not being signalled. She was being seen.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned from the lamps and walked back into the warmth of the carriage. The question the whole train seemed built around was not about a destination. It was about witnessing. The mountain was watching her approach, and the lamps were its eyes. She moved through the swaying cars toward the place where the train would ask her to decide what she was carrying, and what she was ready to leave behind.

The unnameable colour in the lower signal lamp shifted. It became, for one held moment, a colour {~HERO:Vera~} could name: the exact blue of her mother's favourite teacup, the one that had broken the winter she was twelve. The lamp was not signalling the train. It was signalling her. One true, unsettling detail—the mountain knew her memories and was offering one back, cupped in light. She did not know what the offering meant. She did not know what to do with it. But she held the image, the teacup blue, and it was real, and it was hers to carry off the last northbound overnight train of the season. The lamp did not speak again, but it had spoken once, and once was enough.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the passengers gathered to weigh the choice together. They had assembled in the observation car without her noticing—the dining-car regulars, the wakeful child, the counting man, the woman in grey. Not together, exactly, but arrayed through the car like notes on a scale, each occupying a separate seat but all of them facing the same direction: toward {~HERO:Vera~}. The carriage sways and the cold glass holds her reflection over the dark. The child was pleating her blanket. The woman in grey had set her box on the seat beside her. The counting man's lips had stilled. They were waiting.

{~HERO:Vera~} stood in the observation car, facing the passengers gathered to weigh the choice together. The windows here were floor-to-ceiling, and the mountain was visible now, a dark mass shouldering up against the stars. The regulars, the child, the man, the woman—they were not conferring among themselves. They were offering themselves as options. Each one represented a different way through the tunnel. She could approach them as a group and ask them to decide together, pooling their strange wisdoms. Or she could remain where she was, let them remain arrayed before her, and trust that the right guide would speak when the moment came. The last northbound overnight train of the season was slowing, and the mountain was close enough now that she could smell it—cold stone, old water, the mineral patience of deep time.

choices.label: Step up and ask them together.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} walked to the centre of the observation car and addressed the passengers gathered together. 'You've ridden this train before,' she said. 'You've been through the tunnel. Tell me what I need to know.' The dining-car woman in the green shawl spoke first. 'The tunnel takes whatever you are ready to give. But you must give it freely.' The counting man added, 'It does not judge. It receives.' The child looked at {~HERO:Vera~} with her ancient eyes and said, 'You can carry me through, if you want. I'm light.' The woman in grey did not speak, but she placed her hand on the carved box, and {~HERO:Vera~} understood: the woman was offering to share her burden. The fact settled over the group like a shared blanket: the tunnel was not a test. It was a threshold, and the passengers were its keepers.

{~HERO:Vera~} waited. She did not approach the passengers gathered to weigh the choice together; she let them remain in their separate seats, each one a held note in a chord that had not yet resolved. The mountain was close now—the whole train was vibrating with the nearness of the rock. She could stand here and let the right guide reveal themselves, trusting that the night would supply the companion she needed. Or she could let the waiting itself become a surrender, the long minute stretching into a longer one, until the moment of decision passed and the train entered the mountain without her having chosen.

choices.label: Keep the vigil and stay ready.
Let the moment pass you by.

nodes.body: The small wrongness became clear: the passengers gathered to weigh the choice together were not separate beings. They were aspects of the train. The regulars were its patience, the child its memory, the counting man its grief, the woman in grey its tenderness. And they had all been waiting for {~HERO:Vera~} to arrive, because she was the aspect the train did not yet have: the one who chooses. The journey closed around this understanding like a held breath, and the mountain ahead seemed to inhale in sympathy.

{~HERO:Vera~} left the observation car, the gathered passengers receding behind her like figures in a painting she had finished looking at. The question the whole train seemed built around was no longer external. It was inside her, a voice speaking in her own cadence, asking: what will you carry, and what will you set down? She walked toward the mountain tunnel, the rails singing beneath her, the dark mouth opening ahead like a door that had always been waiting.

The passengers gathered to weigh the choice together began to fade. Not physically—they remained in their seats—but {~HERO:Vera~}'s ability to see them began to dim, as though a fog were rising between her and the observation car. She reached out, tried to call to the child, the woman, the counting man, but the fog was cold and thick and her voice came back to her without reaching them. She surfaced later in her own seat, alone, the observation car empty. She was safe. The train was still moving. But the council had dispersed, and the chance to ask her question had passed. The last northbound overnight train of the season rolled on toward the tunnel, and {~HERO:Vera~} rode with it, carrying a silence she had not chosen.

ending.title: No One Will Meet Your Eye

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the conductor at last willing to explain the north line. He had moved to the very front of the train, the vestibule that looked directly into the tunnel's mouth, and his silver punch-clock was fully open now, its face hinged back like a locket. Inside was not a mechanism but a darkness—a small, contained darkness, velvet and deep. The carriage sways and the cold glass holds her reflection over the dark. The conductor's many faces had settled into one: an old man, kind-eyed, carrying the weariness of a long watch faithfully kept. He gestured for her to come closer.

{~HERO:Vera~} stood before the conductor at last willing to explain the north line. The open punch-clock rested in his palms like a chalice. 'The north line,' he said, 'does not end at a station. It ends when a passenger chooses to get off. The track continues. The timetable continues. But the passenger steps off and the line, for them, concludes.' He looked at her with eyes that held every journey he had ever witnessed. 'The tunnel is the place where you decide. On the far side, the train will go on. Whether you go with it—and in what form—is the choice the mountain asks.' {~HERO:Vera~} could ask him now to guide her through directly, to walk beside her in the dark. Or she could let him stand his post and face the tunnel alone, carrying his explanation as a lantern.

choices.label: Ask him to guide you through.
Thank him and face the dark alone.

nodes.body: The conductor nodded slowly. He closed his punch-clock and tucked it under his arm, and the gesture was so ordinary, so human, that {~HERO:Vera~} felt a sudden rush of affection for him—this layered, ancient, dutiful keeper of a clock that held no hours. He did not speak as he led her toward the tunnel mouth, but his presence was steady, a warmth at her shoulder. The fact she carried now was not a riddle but a reassurance: the train had a guardian, and the guardian was real, and he had chosen to walk with her. The tunnel opened ahead, black and vast, and the rails sang a note she could feel in her sternum.

{~HERO:Vera~} thanked the conductor and stepped back. He did not look disappointed; he looked proud. 'You carry enough,' he said, and his voice was warmer than the carriage air. {~HERO:Vera~} stood alone in the vestibule as the train slowed to a walking pace, the mountain's shadow falling across the windows. She could let his explanation be her guide, a compass held in the mind, and trust that she had understood enough to navigate the dark alone. Or she could let the enormity of the tunnel, the cold weight of the stone, the depth of the hour, wash over her until the choice she had been offered dissolved back into the general mystery.

choices.label: Hold the compass and go on alone.
Let the dark dissolve your resolve.

nodes.body: The small wrongness, the one that had followed her all night—it lifted. The conductor's words had not explained the train so much as they had explained {~HERO:Vera~} to herself. She was a passenger, yes. But she was also the one who would decide where the line ended. The journey closed around this understanding not like a held breath but like an embrace. The mountain waited ahead, and the mountain was not a threat. It was a question, and the question was: are you ready?

{~HERO:Vera~} walked toward the tunnel mouth. The question the whole train seemed built around had been given to her, and she had accepted it. The conductor stood behind her, a diminishing figure in the vestibule, his clock closed, his watch complete. Ahead was the dark, and the dark was hers to enter.

The conductor at last willing to explain the north line watched her with his ancient, kind eyes, and then he did something unexpected: he smiled. 'You are not required to understand everything,' he said. 'It is enough that you listened.' He pressed something into her hand—a small metal disc, warm from his pocket, stamped with a symbol she could not identify. A token. Proof of passage. She did not know what it entitled her to, but she closed her fingers around it. One true, unsettling detail, and it was real, and it was hers to carry off the last northbound overnight train of the season. The conductor turned back to his post, and the mountain opened its mouth.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the wakeful child offering to show the way through. The girl had left her seat and stood now in the aisle, barefoot, her blanket trailing from one hand like a surrendered flag. Her ancient eyes were bright, and she held out her other hand to {~HERO:Vera~}. The carriage sways and the cold glass holds her reflection over the dark. The tunnel mouth loomed ahead, a perfect black circle cut into the mountain's face, and the child seemed not to fear it at all. She had walked this dark before. She had walked it many times, and she was offering to walk it again.

{~HERO:Vera~} knelt to meet the wakeful child's eyes. 'You've been through the tunnel,' she said. 'Yes,' the child said. 'I go through every time the train runs. I'm the one who remembers the dark so the other passengers don't have to.' {~HERO:Vera~} understood: the child was not a passenger. She was the train's courage. The part of the journey that knew the dark was passable because it had passed through it already. {~HERO:Vera~} could take the child's hand now and let her lead the way, accepting the gift of borrowed fearlessness. Or she could thank the child and walk alone, carrying only the knowledge that the dark had been crossed before by someone small and barefoot and unafraid.

{~HERO:Vera~} took the child's hand. The girl's palm was warm and slightly sticky, a child's hand, ordinary in every respect except for the steadiness of its grip. She did not speak as she led {~HERO:Vera~} to the vestibule door and out onto the small platform at the front of the carriage, where the wind tore at their clothes and the mountain's shadow swallowed them both. 'It's only dark,' the child said. 'And dark is only a place the light hasn't reached yet. We can reach it.' The fact settled into {~HERO:Vera~} like a warmth spreading from the hand in hers: the tunnel was not an absence. It was a presence, and the child knew its name.

choices.label: Walk into the dark with her.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} smoothed the child's hair back from her forehead. 'Thank you,' she said. 'But I think this time you can rest.' The child looked at her for a long moment, and then she smiled—a small, grave smile that made her look, for an instant, older than the conductor. 'You'll be all right,' she said. It was not a question. She wadded her blanket under her chin and climbed back into her seat, and {~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the tunnel alone. She could carry the child's faith into the dark, a borrowed courage that might hold. Or she could let the weight of the mountain, the cold of the stone, the endless minute before entry, erode that courage until it was only her and the dark and the question of whether she was strong enough.

choices.label: Hold the child's faith and go on.

nodes.body: The small wrongness lifted. The child, whether leading or resting, had done what she was meant to do: she had shown {~HERO:Vera~} that the dark was passable. The journey closed around this new lightness—not a held breath but a released one. The mountain ahead was no longer a barrier. It was a passage, and the passage was old, and many feet had walked it, and hers would be among them.

{~HERO:Vera~} walked toward the tunnel mouth, the child's faith a small, warm stone in her chest. The question the whole train seemed built around had been answered, not with an explanation but with a hand offered in the dark. She stepped forward, and the mountain received her.

The child wriggled her hand free of {~HERO:Vera~}'s and, instead of stepping out into the vestibule, she reached up and tucked the trailing end of her blanket around {~HERO:Vera~}'s shoulders. It was a small gesture, almost absurdly domestic in the shadow of the mountain, but it was the first entirely ordinary kindness the night had offered. {~HERO:Vera~} laughed—a real laugh, quiet but unforced—and the carriage seemed to warm a half-degree around her. The tunnel could wait. The mountain could wait. She was here, on this train, and a child had just tucked a blanket around her like a mother. The doing of it was enough. The night was still strange, but it was no longer cold.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the mourning woman's quiet request to carry a message on. The woman had risen from her table and crossed the carriage to stand before {~HERO:Vera~}, the carved wooden box held in both hands. Her veil was still drawn, but her voice, when she spoke, was clear and low, the voice of someone who had been rehearsing these words for a long time. The carriage sways and the cold glass holds her reflection over the dark. 'I cannot carry her through the tunnel again,' the woman said. 'I have carried her through every season, and I am worn thin. Would you take her? Just to the far side. Just the once.'

{~HERO:Vera~} looked at the box, the carved leaves, the worn edges. The woman's request was not small. To carry the dead through a dark that was already strange, already heavy—it was a weight she had not anticipated lifting. But she had ridden this train all night, and she had seen what it was: a vessel for what could not be carried elsewhere. She could accept the box now, take the woman's daughter in her arms, and carry her through the tunnel as an act of pure witness. Or she could decline, gently, and let the woman find another way—though {~HERO:Vera~} sensed, with a certainty that came from the train itself, that there was no other way, and no other passenger who could do this.

choices.label: Accept the box and carry her.
Decline gently and bear the cost.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} reached out and took the carved box from the woman's hands. It was lighter than she expected. The wood was warm. 'I'll carry her,' {~HERO:Vera~} said. The woman's shoulders dropped—not in collapse but in release, a long-held tension finally unstrung. She pressed her hand to {~HERO:Vera~}'s cheek through the veil, and {~HERO:Vera~} felt the cold of the woman's fingers, the same cold that had been in the conductor's mouth, the same cold that lived in the mountain. 'Her name was Anya,' the woman said. 'Tell the dark her name, and it will let her pass.' The fact settled into {~HERO:Vera~}'s heart: she had been given a name. A name to carry. A name to speak into the stone.

choices.label: Carry the name into the tunnel.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} reached out but did not take the box. She placed her hand over the woman's hand, over the carved leaves. 'I can't,' she said, and her voice was smaller than she wanted it to be. 'I'm not the right person.' The woman did not flinch. She nodded, very slowly, and drew the box back against her chest. 'It is all right,' she said, though her voice said it was not. {~HERO:Vera~} could hold this refusal, the weight of it, and let it teach her something about what she was—and was not—capable of carrying. Or she could let the shame of the refusal, the hollow guilt of turning away from a grieving mother, pull her under into a sleep where such choices did not exist.

choices.label: Hold the refusal and learn from it.
Let the guilt take you under.

nodes.body: The small wrongness lifted. Whether {~HERO:Vera~} had accepted the box or refused it, the woman's request had changed something. The journey closed around this new understanding: grief could be shared, or it could be witnessed, and both were forms of carrying. The mountain ahead was a place where the living and the dead could pass together, or where the living could pass alone, carrying only the knowledge that they had been asked and had answered—in whatever way they could.

{~HERO:Vera~} walked toward the tunnel mouth, the carved box in her arms or the weight of refusal in her chest—both were heavy, and both were hers. The question the whole train seemed built around had become specific. It was no longer 'what is this train?' but 'what will you carry, and for whom?' She stepped forward into the mountain's shadow, and the dark received her.

{~HERO:Vera~} carried the carved wooden box through the tunnel. The dark was absolute, the sound of the wheels a muffled roar, but the box was warm in her arms and she did not feel alone. When she emerged on the far side, the first grey dawn was breaking over the peaks, and the woman in grey was standing on the platform—the real platform, the wooden one, the one that existed under the cold morning sky. She took the box from {~HERO:Vera~}'s arms and held it against her heart. 'You carried her home,' she said. 'You carried us both.' {~HERO:Vera~} stepped down from the train and felt the platform boards solid under her feet. Something long carried was finally set down. The last northbound overnight train of the season exhaled steam behind her, and the dawn held.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the timetable whose columns of stations never end. It hung in a glass case bolted to the wall of the vestibule, its pages yellow and brittle, the type so small it blurred unless she pressed her nose nearly to the glass. The columns ran down and down, page after page, station after station, and she could see that the last entry on the last page was not a name. It was an ellipsis. The carriage sways and the cold glass holds her reflection over the dark. The timetable was still being written. As she watched, a new line of type flickered into existence at the bottom of the final column—a station that had not been there a moment before.

choices.label: Press closer to the glass case.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} studied the timetable whose columns of stations never end. The new line, the one that had just appeared, was not a station. It was a question mark. The timetable did not know what came next. It was waiting for her to decide. She could read deeper into the endless columns, trace the route backward through all the stations that had come before, searching for a pattern that might tell her what to choose. Or she could accept that the timetable was not a guide but a mirror—it showed her only what she had already travelled—and let the train's own momentum carry her into the unwritten space.

choices.label: Read the columns for a clue.
Let the unwritten space remain open.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} read the endless timetable, line by line, and among the thousands of station names she found one she knew. Her own. Not the station where she was born, but the platform where she boarded tonight. It was listed in the column for three winters ago, under a different train number, with a small footnote: 'passenger disembarked. journey incomplete.' She had ridden this train before. Or a version of her had. And she had gotten off too early. The fact lodged in her mind like a key turning in a lock she had not known was there: the last northbound overnight train of the season was a second chance, and the unwritten space ahead was the ending she had not stayed for the first time.

{~HERO:Vera~} stepped back from the endless timetable. She did not need to read it. The fact that it existed, that it was still being written, was enough. The columns could keep unspooling, station after station, an infinity of possibilities. She could hold that openness as a comfort—the journey did not have to end, the last page did not have to be written—and walk into the tunnel carrying that openness like a lantern. Or she could let the vertigo of the endless columns, the sheer scale of the unwritten, overwhelm her ability to choose at all.

choices.label: Hold the openness and go on.

nodes.body: The small wrongness came clear: the timetable whose columns of stations never end was not a schedule. It was a record of every passenger who had ever ridden this train, and every choice they had made at the tunnel. Some had gotten off. Some had ridden through. Some were still riding, their names still appearing in new columns, year after year. {~HERO:Vera~} was already in the timetable. Her name was there, printed in the same small type as all the rest, and the line beside it was blank. The journey closed around this understanding like a held breath, and the mountain ahead seemed to lean close, waiting.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned from the endless timetable and walked toward the tunnel mouth. The question the whole train seemed built around was no longer a mystery. It was a choice, and the choice was hers alone, and the timetable was waiting to record it. She stepped forward, and the dark wrote her name on its blank page.

The columns of the endless timetable began to multiply. New pages grew before her eyes, the glass case filling with paper, then overflowing—the timetable was no longer a document but a tide, rising around her ankles, her knees, her waist. Station names she had never seen, in languages she could not read, poured past her in an endless flood. She tried to hold on to one name, one fixed point, but the tide was too strong. She surfaced later in her seat, the timetable case dark and still, the glass reflecting only her own tired face. She was safe. The train was still moving. But the moment when she might have chosen her station, written her own name in the column, had been swept away in the flood of all the other choices, all the other passengers, all the other journeys that had no end.

Vera stood in the coupling space between two carriages, the cold air whistling through the rubber seals, and understood the first bottleneck: the last northbound overnight train of the season never arrived because it was not travelling toward a destination. It was travelling toward a condition. Every clock aboard had stopped at eleven minutes past midnight—not broken, but resting. The north terminus remained exactly one hour off no matter how many miles the wheels ate. The journey was not a line; it was a layer. The train was passing through the same hour over and over, deepening into it, and the passengers who had ridden longest were the ones who had learned to stop measuring the deepening. Vera had four ways into the next layer, four passengers whose knowledge might open a door the timetable could not show her. She chose.

choices.label: Find the child who never sleeps.

nodes.body: Vera stood in the centre of the dining car and looked at the faces around her. The second bottleneck had opened. Who were these passengers, really? Not travellers. Not commuters. Each one was riding for a reason older than tonight, a reason that had a shape and a weight and a season of its own. The dining-car regulars were remnants of journeys that had ended long ago; the child was the train's own memory given a voice; the counting man was the railway's grief; the woman in grey was the living bond that kept a dead girl on the route. None of them would say where they first got on, because the answer was not a station. The answer was a loss. And Vera had come far enough into the night that she could now ask them a harder question—one that might show her what lay ahead, in the mountain's shadow.

The train slowed to a walking pace. The mountain filled the windows, a wall of granite and old snow, and the tunnel mouth opened ahead like a held note. The last northbound overnight train of the season was approaching the third bottleneck, and {~HERO:Vera~} stood in the vestibule with the cold glass against her palm and the roaring dark just beyond the door. She had to decide what she would carry through, and what she would leave. The conductor could tell her the truth—the whole truth, without evasion, if she demanded it. The child could lead her, hand in hers, the dark made manageable by small, steady footsteps. The mourning woman's request was still open, a box and a name waiting to be borne. The timetable, endlessly scrolling, held a line for her if she looked. The mountain would not wait forever. The train was already entering the shadow.

choices.label: Ask the conductor for the whole truth.
Let the child lead you by the hand.
Answer the mourning woman's quiet request to carry a message on.
Search the endless timetable for your line.

nodes.body: The tunnel ended not in a burst of light but in a gradual lifting of the darkness, a thinning of the black until it was grey, and then the grey touched the peaks and became the first grey dawn. The train emerged onto a high mountain shelf, the rails clinging to a ledge above a valley still drowned in shadow. The passengers—the regulars, the child, the counting man, the woman in grey—were all standing now, their faces turned toward the light. And {~HERO:Vera~} understood, with a clarity that felt like cold water, that the last northbound overnight train of the season was not a route but a passage, and the passage was ending, and how it ended—what she did with the last of the night—was now hers to shape. The dawn was holding its breath. The train was waiting.

choices.label: Ride on and simply be present.
Turn to the traveler who needs you.
Chase the last of the truth.
Try to get off before the mountain tunnel.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} chose to stop striving. She found a seat by the window and simply let the train carry her. The carriage narrowed to this one long, lucid stretch of track before the mountain tunnel, the rails gleaming in the grey pre-light, the peaks sharp against the brightening sky. She did not interrogate the passengers. She did not study the letter or read the timetable or press the conductor for answers. She sat, and she breathed, and she let the journey be what it was. The last northbound overnight train of the season rocked gently over a switch, and {~HERO:Vera~} felt her own heartbeat slow to match the rhythm of the wheels.

choices.label: Follow the rhythm toward the dawn.

nodes.body: In the plain act of riding on, wide awake, Vera found two doors waiting. One was small and close and immediate: she could let the peace of the moment be enough, seal the night here, and step off into the dawn with the memory of a quiet journey held whole. The other was larger, further, still open: she could stay with the train past this first thinning of the dark, let the peace deepen into something she did not yet have a name for, and ride all the way into the full light. The window beside her was cold, but the glass was no longer a mirror. It was a window. She could see out.

choices.label: Stay open to the growing light.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} rode on, the peace settling deeper into her bones with every mile. The train curved along the mountain ledge, and the valley below began to fill with light—gold first, then rose, then a clear, pale blue that seemed to have no source, as though the sky itself were simply waking. The carriage was quiet. The passengers were still. {~HERO:Vera~} came level with the first grey dawn coming up over the ridgeline, and all the night's threads seemed to gather in her hands—not tangled, but laid parallel, a weaving that was almost complete. She only had to make the final pass.

choices.label: Meet the dawn at the ridgeline.

nodes.body: The peace {~HERO:Vera~} had found was real, but it was not transferable. She tried to hold it as the train slowed for the station—a small, unnamed stop, a wooden platform under a grey sky—but the moment she stood to gather her case, the peace dissolved. It had been a product of the motion, of the carriage's steady rock and the glass's cold surface under her palm, and the stillness of the platform killed it. She stepped down onto the boards and felt the quiet she had carried evaporate, leaving only a residue of loss. The train pulled away northward without her, and the sight of its tail light receding into the thinning dark was the loneliest thing she had ever seen.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned toward the traveler at the carriage end who needed a hand. She had not noticed her before—a young woman, perhaps her own age, curled into a seat with her arms wrapped around herself as though holding something in. Her face was turned to the window, but her reflection in the glass showed eyes that were wide and frightened. The carriage narrowed to this one long, lucid stretch of track before the mountain tunnel, and {~HERO:Vera~} understood that she had been riding all night toward this: a passenger who could not carry herself through the dark. She crossed the aisle and knelt beside the seat.

choices.label: Follow the impulse toward the dawn.

nodes.body: The traveler looked at Vera with eyes that were the colour of the grey dawn outside. 'I can't go through the dark alone,' she whispered. 'I've been riding this train every season, and I always get off before the tunnel. I'm afraid of what I'll find on the other side.' Vera understood. The tunnel was not only darkness. It was revelation. And revelation was easier to avoid than to face. She could stay with this traveler, walk beside her through the dark, and risk her own arrival being delayed—or forfeited entirely. Or she could close the choice here, give the traveler a kind word and a blanket, and step down before the tunnel claimed her own journey too.

choices.label: Give her the blanket and step off.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} took the traveler's hand and together they walked through the vestibule and into the tunnel's mouth. The dark was absolute, but the hand in hers was warm and trembling, and {~HERO:Vera~} found that focusing on that trembling—steadying it, soothing it—steadied her in return. The tunnel was long, longer than it had seemed from the outside, but they walked it together, and when the first grey dawn broke over the peaks on the far side, the traveler was still holding her hand, and her eyes were no longer frightened. {~HERO:Vera~} came level with the ridgeline where all the night's threads gathered, and the thread she had chosen to carry was another person's courage.

{~HERO:Vera~} wrapped her own coat around the traveler's shoulders and pressed a warm cup of tea from the dining car into her hands. 'You'll be all right,' {~HERO:Vera~} said, and she meant it. But the traveler looked at her with those grey-dawn eyes and said, 'You're leaving.' It was not a question. {~HERO:Vera~} stepped down onto the platform as the train slowed for the mountain's approach, and watched the carriages slide past her one by one. The traveler's face appeared in a window, small and pale, and then the window was gone. The train entered the tunnel, and {~HERO:Vera~} was left alone on the platform in the cold grey dawn, the hand she had almost taken now forever untaken.

ending.title: The Hand You Did Not Take

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} drew the stranger's letter from her coat. She had read it once, but she had not read it fully—the last lines, the cramped writing at the bottom of the page, had been too dense, too faint. She held it to the grey window light as the carriage narrowed to this one long, lucid stretch of track before the mountain tunnel. Outside, the peaks were emerging from the dark, their ridges sharpening against the sky. Inside, the letter's final paragraph resolved: a string of names, written in a hand that trembled slightly, each name struck through except the last. Her own name. Not struck through. Waiting.

choices.label: Follow the final lines toward the dawn.

nodes.body: The unread lines held a question. The stranger had written: 'If you are reading this, you have already chosen to stay on the train. The next choice is whether you want to know why the train exists, or whether it is enough to know that it does, and that it carries you.' The small door was to close the letter now, fold it away, and accept the mystery as a gift—the train was here, the night was passing, the dawn was coming, and the reasons could remain the train's own business. The larger door was to read on, to learn the origin of the last northbound train, and to accept that the knowledge would change her—and that she could not unlearn it once it was hers.

choices.label: Read the last of the truth.
Fold the letter and let the mystery be.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} read the last lines. The stranger had written that the last northbound overnight train of the season had been built not of steel and steam but of accumulated departures—every goodbye that had ever been spoken on a railway platform, every journey begun with a heart too heavy to leave but too restless to stay. The train was the sum of all those leave-takings, given form and rhythm and a route that went north because north was the direction of endings, and endings were what the train existed to help its passengers reach. {~HERO:Vera~} came level with the first grey dawn and understood that she was not a passenger. She was a goodbye, and the train was carrying her home.

choices.label: Meet the dawn with the truth in your hands.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} read enough. She read that the train was kind, and that it travelled through a space between the world and the world's memory, and that the passengers were all people who had left something behind and needed a journey to teach them how to set it down. She did not read the final lines—the ones that told why the train had chosen her specifically. It was enough to know that it had, and that the choosing was not arbitrary. She folded the letter, tucked it into the seat cushion where she had found it, and stepped off the train at the mountain station with half a mystery cupped in her hands and a quiet, abiding peace that she did not need the other half.

{~HERO:Vera~} walked to the cold vestibule door and placed her hand on the iron handle. The train was slowing now, the brakes sighing against the wheels, and she could see a small platform ahead—just a wooden deck and a single lamp burning yellow in the grey pre-dawn. She could step down here. She could end the journey before the mountain tunnel, before the dark pressed its question, before she had to decide what she was carrying and what she was ready to leave. The carriage narrowed to this one long, lucid stretch of track before the mountain tunnel, and the door was cold but the handle turned easily.

choices.label: Follow the urge to step down.

nodes.body: The cold vestibule door and the idea of stepping down presented two doors of their own. The smaller one: she could step off now, onto the quiet platform under the grey sky, and let the train slip away into the tunnel without her. She would be safe. She would be on solid ground. And she would never know what the dark had been waiting to show her. The larger door: she could close the vestibule door, turn her back on the platform, and walk back into the warmth of the carriage. She could ride into the tunnel. She could choose the unknown. The lamp on the platform flickered, and the train's brakes released slightly, as though the engine itself were asking.

choices.label: Close the door and stay aboard.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} closed the vestibule door. The latch caught with a solid thunk, and the train seemed to exhale—steam or relief, she could not tell. She walked back through the swaying cars, past the quiet passengers, past the child and the conductor and the woman in grey, and took her seat by the window. The platform slid past, then fell away, and the mountain rose before her. She had chosen the unknown. The first grey dawn was touching the peaks, and {~HERO:Vera~} came level with the ridgeline where all the night's threads gathered, and she was not afraid.

The door opened onto a platform {~HERO:Vera~} recognised. It was the platform. The first one. The sleet had stopped, the snow had stopped, and the clock above the waiting room was still frozen at eleven minutes past midnight—but it was her clock, her station, the boards she had crossed only a few hours ago. The last northbound overnight train of the season pulled away behind her, its tail lights dwindling into a grey dawn that should have been further north, should have been on the far side of a mountain. But she was here. She had circled back. The night was unspent, and the journey had refused to end because she had refused to finish it. She stood on the platform, her case in her hand, and watched the train she had been too afraid to ride disappear into a mist that was not entirely weather.

The train reached the high point of the line, a ledge carved into the mountain's shoulder where the rails curved around a final spur of rock and the whole northern valley opened below. The first grey dawn was no longer grey: the peaks were going gold, the snowfields catching fire, the shadows retreating into the deepest folds of the range. The passengers were quiet, each one turned toward the light, and {~HERO:Vera~} understood that this was the true bottleneck—the place where every route through the night gathered, every thread she had followed, every question she had asked of the conductor and the child and the letter and the land. The journey's last shape waited on one final turning. She could set the night down, or carry it forward. She could give, or receive. She could name what she had learned, or ask only for mercy. The train slowed, and the light held.

choices.label: Set the night down and stay.
Give a fellow traveler your seat.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} stopped trying to arrive. She let the north terminus stay one hour off forever, a destination that existed only as a direction, a north that would always recede before her, and she found, at last, that she did not mind the distance. The train was not late. It was exactly where it was meant to be, and so was she. She leaned her forehead against the cold glass and watched the peaks turn from gold to rose to the clear, depthless blue of a mountain morning, and the watching was its own arrival. The journey had been the point all along.

choices.label: Make peace with the infinite journey.

nodes.body: The seat beside the mourning woman was still warm, though she had risen and moved to the window to watch the dawn. {~HERO:Vera~} understood that the offer was still open: she could stay beside this woman through the tunnel, through the rest of the journey, and give up her own arrival in the process. The mountain tunnel would take whatever she offered, and if she offered her destination, the train would let her ride forever in the woman's company, a comfort that asked only for the comfort of her presence. Or she could step back, keep her arrival, and let the woman ride on alone—a kindness measured, a boundary held, a loss accepted.

choices.label: Stay too long and lose yourself.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} stood and faced the window. The glass was cold and the view was vast—the whole northern valley, the receding dark, the train's own steam rising into the golden light. She spoke the north terminus's quiet truth aloud, not to the passengers or the conductor, but to the grey window, to her own reflection, to the journey itself. She named what the train was: a passage for the unarrived, a vessel for the departed, a kindness extended across the seasons to anyone who needed a night to carry what the day could not hold. And the naming of it was its own kind of arrival. The words settled in the cold air of the carriage and did not dissipate. They stayed.

{~HERO:Vera~} closed her eyes. She had asked enough questions, chased enough threads, carried enough of other people's grief and mystery and memory. She asked the last northbound overnight train of the season for nothing but a safe waking. Not understanding, not revelation, not the true name of the north terminus or the origin of the light in the signal lamps. Just safety. Just morning. And the train, being kinder than she had feared, granted exactly that. The carriage warmed, the wheels found a gentle rhythm, and the gold of the dawn softened into a plain, ordinary daylight that asked nothing of her at all.

{~HERO:Vera~} rode the last northbound overnight train of the season into the full morning with open eyes and an open heart. The peaks were bright now, the valley filled with a mist that was breaking into ribbons of cloud, and the passengers—the regulars, the child, the counting man, the woman in grey—had settled into a quiet fellowship, each one at peace with what they carried. {~HERO:Vera~} felt the night's last threads loosen and fall away. She was not the same person who had boarded at the platform, under the stopped clock and the turning sleet. She was the person the journey had made her, and the person the journey had made her was finally, wholly here. The train did not arrive at a station. It arrived at a condition: the condition of being present, of being ready, of being done with fleeing. The north terminus was this moment, and the moment held. She sat in the warm carriage, the gold light on her face, and she was home—not because the train had stopped, but because she had.

{~HERO:Vera~} stayed beside the mourning woman through the mountain tunnel and delivered her safely into the first grey dawn. The carved box was heavy in {~HERO:Vera~}'s arms, but the weight was not only stone and silence—it was the weight of a promise kept, a daughter borne home, a journey completed not for herself but for another. The woman walked beside her, her veil lifted now, her face a map of grief that was no longer solitary. When they emerged from the tunnel, the platform was small and wooden and lit by a single lamp that guttered in the morning wind, and the woman stepped down onto it and turned back to look at {~HERO:Vera~}. 'You carried us both,' she said. 'Now go and carry yourself.' {~HERO:Vera~} stood in the doorway of the train and watched the woman walk away into the brightening valley, and she understood that helping another home had been her own arrival all along. The train's whistle blew softly, a note of farewell or of celebration, and {~HERO:Vera~} climbed back aboard and smiled at the dawn.

{~HERO:Vera~} stayed beside the mourning woman past the tunnel, past the first grey dawn, past the second and the third. The train continued north, and the woman continued to need her, and {~HERO:Vera~} continued to give. She gave until she was hollow, until the dawns blurred together into a pale wash of light she no longer registered, until her own name felt like a word in a foreign language. The traveler was helped—the carved box was borne, the daughter was delivered—but {~HERO:Vera~} surfaced on a platform she did not recognise, under a sky that was neither light nor dark, and she did not know how long she had been riding. The good deed was real. It mattered. But it had cost her the journey, and the cost was heavier than she had known it would be.

{~HERO:Vera~} spoke the north terminus's name aloud, and the name was not a place. It was a condition: the state of being ready to stop running, ready to turn and face the thing you had been fleeing, ready to set it down. The last northbound overnight train of the season was the vessel that carried travellers to that condition, season after season, and the tunnel was the passage where the setting-down happened. {~HERO:Vera~} did not stay on the train forever. The dawn came fully, and the train pulled into a station—a real one, with a wooden platform and a stationmaster who looked up from his newspaper and nodded as though he had been expecting her. She stepped down. But she left knowing, and the knowing settled something in her that had been unsettled for a very long time. The train's whistle blew twice, a departing call, and {~HERO:Vera~} stood on the platform and let the sound wash over her without needing to follow it.

{~HERO:Vera~} woke at her own quiet station. The train had stopped, though she did not remember the braking or the steam or the conductor's final call. She was simply sitting on a bench on a platform she knew, her case at her feet, the sky above her a clean, unhaunted blue. She was unharmed. She was awake. The last northbound overnight train of the season was gone, and the night it had carried was gone with it, unexplained and irretrievable. She stood slowly, her legs stiff, her mind full of images that were already beginning to fade—a child's ancient eyes, a leaf-carved box, a punch-clock full of turning darkness. She had been offered a door, and she had chosen not to walk through it. The choice was hers. The safety was hers. But she carried, and would carry for a long time, the sense of that unchosen door waiting behind her in a night that still, if she closed her eyes, seemed to be swaying gently back and forth on iron rails.
